newsitem.title: USA: UK's Pearson acquires US publisher Putnam Berkley.
newsitem.headline: UK's Pearson acquires US publisher Putnam Berkley.

text.p: International media group Pearson said Tuesday its Penguin books unit has acquired Putnam Berkley, a leading U.S. publisher of popular fiction, from MCA Inc. for $336 million.
The merger will make Penguin the second-largest English language trade book publisher in the world and the third-largest in the United States, where its market share will double to 12 percent.
The move adds contemporary writers such as Tom Clancy, Patricia Cornwell and Kurt Vonnegut to Penguin's powerful back catalogue of famous authors and established titles.
"The combination of Penguin and Putnam will create a powerhouse in both the frontlist and backlist," Penguin Group Chief Executive-designate Michael Lynton told Reuters.
British-based Pearson's media empire includes the Financial Times newspaper. MCA is Seagram Co.'s entertainment arm.
Pearson said the acquisition would boost its earnings from the first year.

"Because Penguin USA and Putnam are of a like size there is tremendous potential for cost savings," said Lynton, the former head of Disney's Hollywood Pictures. He will take over as boss of Penguin at the start of the year.
Pearson is also in a state of transition. Texan Marjorie Scardino will take over as chief executive in January, the first woman to head a leading British firm.

Industry analysts are scrutinising every move Pearson makes for clues as to the course the company will follow under Scardino as it seeks to focus its activities more tightly. Market reaction was muted, with Pearson shares edging up 1p (1.7 cents) to 751p ($12.62) in a firmer market.

"Is it a signal that Pearson is building in areas where it has a strong position but where there are not particularly attractive long-term growth prospects?" said Anthony de Larrinaga of Panmure Gordon.
Lynton said he was confident about the prospects for the book market. "In this world of changing technologies, books appear to be a constant. I'm pretty bullish about the situation," he said.
But his enthusiasm was not initially shared by Standard & Poor's Corp., which said it may cut Pearson's debt ratings because of the "negative financial impact of the deal."

Pearson has a mixed record with recent acquisitions and is still trying to turn around U.S. consumer software company Mindscape, which has plunged into a loss following its $462 million purchase in 1994.

Pearson Finance Director John Makinson said the company was "more than comfortable with the price" paid for Putnam, which had net sales of $276 million and operating profit of $34 million in its last financial year.
He said the purchase still left Pearson with plenty of room for manoeuvre. "I don't think that the size of this acquisition precludes us from doing something else," he said.
